item.title: Ex-Bangladesh PM Hasina says fear won’t stop her from going home. [ dawn ]
item.description:
NEW DELHI: Bangladesh’s fugitive ex-prime minister Sheikh Hasina said on Wednesday she would return to her country in December even if it meant imprisonment, insisting “fear cannot decide” her “duty to the people”.

“I may be detained, I may be sent to prison. But fear cannot decide my duty to the people,” Hasina, 78, said in an audio broadcast to a packed press club in New Delhi.

“I cannot stay away while my beloved countrymen are suffering,” added Hasina, who is in hiding in India. She was speaking on the second anniversary since her iron-fisted rule was overthrown on August 5, 2024 by a student-led uprising.

Hasina fled by helicopter to India as crowds stormed her palace. The United Nations says up to 1,400 people were killed in crackdowns as she tried to cling to power.

In November 2025, a court in Dhaka found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to be hanged. Dhaka has formally requested Hasina’s extradition, which New Delhi has said was “under examination”.

Hasina said she wanted to return in December as it marks the month Bangladesh gained independence in 1971. But her comments on Wednesday elicited anger in Dhaka where protesters burnt her effigy.

Her remarks echoed comments in an interview in July in which she said she wanted to return to Bangladesh by the year’s end. “I may be killed. I may be arrested. I may be sent to prison,” Hasina wrote, in an email sent from hiding. “I am fully aware of my fate. Still, I want to go back because my people are calling me.”

The Bangladeshi government has said it will ensure Hasina receives due legal process in all cases against her should she return. Rights groups have long accused Hasina’s former administration of abuses including the murder of rivals, suppression of opposition parties, rigged courts and one-sided elections. Tens of thousands of people watched the address broadcast online.

Bangladeshi authorities have banned local media from airing her speech.

Published in Dawn, August 6th, 2026

item.title: Rising concrete, drowned cities. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
By the time the water pulls back from the narrow alleys of Khatunganj, Chittagong's bustling wholesale commodity hub, it has already done its accounting: A grey line halfway up the shop shutters, a skin of silt across the floor.
For merchants like Jalaluddin, a mid-sized trader of lentils and spices in these lanes, a heavy July downpour no longer means a temporary halt; it means a calculated loss. The downpour was heavy, certainly, but predictable. A monsoon city has no excuse for being surprised by the monsoon.
What he did not bargain for is a road outside that has been raised so many times his threshold now sits a step below it. Jalaluddin is not fighting the sky; he is living at the bottom of a concrete bowl the city built around him.
This urban drowning is normalized as an inevitable act of nature, ignoring that it is a crisis by design.
Why our cities are being drowned
For years, we have pointed at the sky, blaming unprecedented rainfall, upstream runoff, climate change, and the plain misfortune of living on a delta. But looking exclusively at the sky misses the point.
While shifting climate patterns do trigger more intense bursts of rain, treating waterlogging as a purely meteorological crisis overlooks the physical reality on the ground. Our drainage architecture has reached the limit of what it was built to carry.
Dhaka’s network, for instance, was designed to handle a mere 10 to 15 millimetres of rain per hour, a threshold an ordinary monsoon morning easily crosses.
Yet, heavy rain alone cannot explain why geographically distinct cities experience identical bottlenecks. The real issue is developing slowly beneath our feet: Urban land subsidence.
Decades of chaotic growth have forced pumping massive volumes of drinking water from deep underground, causing the water table to drop by roughly two metres every year in dense urban areas.
As these aquifers deplete, the soft delta sediments compact, causing the surface to settle. Satellite data confirms that parts of both Dhaka and Chittagong are gradually settling. This shifting topography complicates traditional engineering.
Drainage relies on gravity and accurate slopes. When the city sinks while the receiving river networks maintain their baseline, the drainage gradient flattens. Pumping water out becomes physically impossible. Simply raising roads or building higher embankments offers temporary relief when the very ground beneath them is settling lower.
Diverse terrain, uniform failure
What is most striking is how this exact pattern of failure replicates itself across the country, independent of local geography.
Bangladesh's major urban centres feature radically different terrains, yet they demonstrate an identical vulnerability to the rain. Dhaka is a flat, river-bound metropolis; Chittagong is defined by coastal hills and tidal dynamics. Sylhet occupies a rain-heavy northeastern depression, Khulna sits on a low coastal delta, and Comilla spans the eastern plains.
Despite these geographic contrasts, the fundamental vulnerability in each city stems from the gradual reduction of natural water-retention spaces.
In Dhaka, essential wetlands and retention ponds have been steadily swallowed by built-up real estate. In Chittagong, rampant hill-cutting flushes loose topsoil into the drainage network, rapidly silting up the city’s canal networks and rendering them ineffective when tides run high. The topography changes, but the underlying philosophy is the same: Treating natural water-retention spaces as land waiting to be paved over.
The invisible toll
Beyond the familiar television footage of gridlocked, waterlogged streets lies an invisible economic toll that national accounting mostly misses.
A city paralyzed by stormwater means millions of lost labour hours as workers remain trapped in static traffic or stranded at home. While major corporate entities insulate themselves with insurance policies and sprawling supply chains, small and medium enterprises, the actual spine of the urban economy, carry the brunt of the crisis without a safety net. For a neighbourhood grocer or a localized trader, one severe waterlogging event can wipe out their whole working capital overnight.
And when the city raises the road, as it did outside that Khatunganj wholesale market shop, the floodwater does not magically vanish. It is simply pushed out of public view, away from the news cameras, and directly into private stockrooms. There, behind closed shutters, the owner is forced to absorb the ruin alone or turn to high-interest informal loans just to restock.
The financial erosion does not stop on the shop floor; it compromises public health, education, and basic utilities. School closures disrupt the academic calendars, inflicting a permanent setback on students.
Emergency care grinds to a halt on submerged roads. When a flooded intersection delays an ambulance, transforming a manageable medical emergency into a fatality, the tragedy is absent from official city records.
Simultaneously, critical telecommunications infrastructure experiences higher operating costs as base stations flood, and municipal utilities spend millions repairing water-damaged infrastructure, driving up baseline maintenance expenditures.
The crisis has now penetrated the financial sector. Domestic insurance companies are restructuring premiums and denying coverage to properties located within chronic flooding zones, leaving whole communities financially exposed.
Institutional efforts to quantify these compounding failures remain alarmingly thin. The Bangladesh Institute of Planners estimates that the damage from waterlogging together with traffic gridlock sits at roughly Tk 12,000 crore annually, a baseline figure that heavily underestimates the real damage.
Because the state does not systematically track these cascading socio-economic impacts, they remain invisible during national budget allocations. Ultimately, what goes unmeasured is treated as nonexistent, leaving the crisis permanently unfinanced and unresolved.
The construction trap
Persistent urban flooding across Bangladesh is not driven by a lack of capital investment. Dhaka’s two city corporations built and overhauled more than 334 kilometres of drains and box culverts between 2021 and 2024, representing a fraction of Tk 1,316 crore funneled into capital drainage over over five years.
Chittagong is currently deploying four massive flood-mitigation initiatives valued nearly Tk 14,000 crore, of which over Tk 10,000 crore has already been spent, yet its commercial wards still left chest-deep in stormwater this year.
Similarly, Khulna has spent roughly Tk 750 crore of a Tk 823 crore drainage modernization scheme, yet the city experiences the same failures. The shortfall lies in what we choose to build with that money.
Our city planning is obsessed with visible capital works, building new assets that offer easy ribbon-cutting ceremonies, while long-term operations are systematically starved. But an unmaintained drain is worse than no drain at all.
A sluice gate left without regular clearance becomes an artificial dam; a box culvert built without structural access hatches inevitably chokes on subterranean solid waste.
Khulna illustrates the absurdity of this approach perfectly. Most of the drains built under its latest modernization scheme were covered without any automated way to clean them, so routine repairs now rely on municipal workers lifting heavy concrete slabs by hand.
The structural failure runs even deeper, aggravated by a complete lack of inter-utility coordination. Lacking a centralized spatial database, individual agencies independently slice water mains and fiber-optic cables straight through active drainage arteries, creating internal mesh that traps debris and paralyzes water flow.
Despite this, because municipal progress is audited through abstract indicators like “kilometres built” or “percentage complete,” these mega-projects are hailed as absolute triumphs. They are celebrated as nearly finished the very same week that the surrounding neighborhoods go underwater. In our current bureaucratic calculus, whether a city stays dry is the one performance metric never actually measured.
A fragmented urban mandate
Behind every flooded street is a fractured governance model. Handing primary drainage control from central water authorities to local city corporations has reshuffled administrative titles, but it hasn't dried up a single road.
Stormwater management across any given urban basin remains split among municipal corporations, development authorities, water boards, and isolated utilities. The institutional neglect is systemic. Half a decade after inheriting the capital’s drainage portfolio, Dhaka South operates without a single department dedicated to waterlogging.
Across the boundary, Dhaka North reports that sizeable pockets of its own jurisdiction drain through systems it does not control. When every agency owns only a fraction of the line, failures are inevitably blamed on the next office over. Pass-the-buck bureaucracy has effectively replaced structural maintenance across Bangladesh.
Institutional neglect is reinforced by an economic model that disincentivizes conservation. According to urban planning assessments, the natural water-retention footprint across our major cities has collapsed over the last three decades; in Dhaka alone, the official Detailed Area Plan records surface water bodies shrinking from 20.57% of the city's surface area in 1995 to just 2.9% by 2023.
A natural pond performs vital storm-buffering services without ever appearing on a municipal balance sheet. Conversely, the moment that retention space is filled with earth, it transforms into taxable real estate.
Because municipal frameworks monetize the reclaimed plot while ignoring the economic devastation of a drowned neighborhood, predatory reclamation remains the default business model nationwide from Chittagong to Sylhet.
Regulatory enforcement is frequently crippled by local influence, keeping this cycle alive no matter how many new capital projects are announced. Yet the path forward does not require reinventing our cities.
Researchers at the River and Delta Research Centre estimate that recovering and reconnecting just 15 of Dhaka’s main encroached canals could remove up to 80% of its recurrent monsoon waterlogging.
The hydrology of our delta hubs remains very predictable. The water still remembers its natural path; we have simply chosen to build over the roads it used to take.
The cost of stalled cargo
Beyond domestic inconvenience, this vulnerability is a direct threat to international confidence. A country actively positioning itself as a reliable alternative for global manufacturing supply chains cannot afford unpredictable infrastructure.
Yet, every monsoon, global buyers and prospective investors are greeted with images of flooded export processing zones and cargo truck logjams on submerged trade corridors. When a shipment of ready-made garments misses its vessel because a primary highway goes underwater, the damage to our national reliability is immediate and self-inflicted.
Foreign investors do not care about the distinction between global climate shifts and local municipal failures; they simply look at whether a country can keep its infrastructure functional. A national reputation, much like a natural wetland, is incredibly cheap to lose and exceptionally slow to rebuild.
Learning to hold the water
Over the next decade, we must begin dismantling our fractured urban bureaucracy. We need unified, metropolitan watershed authorities with the legal power to bypass local patronage and treat the drainage network as a single, living organ. Alongside this enforcement, the state must aggressively reclaim and dredge the historical canal networks that once served as the natural arteries of our cities.
A watershed authority without a budget for operation, however, will only inherit the same decay at a higher grade. Chittagong is the warning. Its mega projects are nearing completion with no structured plan to sustain the infrastructure, leaving critical workforce and funding recommendations ignored.
The city corporation has been forced to propose a separate Tk 322 crore scheme just to clean and maintain the 36 canals it is inheriting, a scramble for funding after the fact, rather than including into the original approval. Yet, that same corporation cannot even clean its current 1,600 kilometers of drains and 57 canals due to an ongoing lack of machinery.
Long-term custody is treated as a secondary problem to be financed later. Maintenance should be a condition of approval: No drainage asset sign off without a named operator and a decade of locked-in funding.
Our institutions ignore the connection between what we build and what we pump. Because drainage and water supply are handled by separate agencies with independent budgets, the resulting policy is totally fragmented.
It is a vicious, self-inflicted loop: We blanket the surface in concrete, block natural rainwater recharge, and drill deeper into a collapsing aquifer. As the ground subsides, our multi-crore drainage networks lose their vital slopes. A single, consolidated watershed authority would treat the water cycle as an unbroken loop, halting emergency drilling to force the finishing of surface plants, and regulating private tube wells under one centralized authority.
The relentless encroachment on surviving wetlands is a severe economic crime against our urban future, not a bureaucratic oversight. Yet, alongside this enforcement gap lies another blind spot: Our obsession with trendy global planning models.
The “sponge city” concept is frequently urged upon Dhaka, but its long-term operational costs are completely ignored. Permeable infrastructure functions only as long as its pores remain open.
In a delta city, dust and silt rapidly clog these surfaces, demanding an expensive regime of vacuum sweeping and pressure washing. The reality is grim: The city administrations that cannot even clear its existing 2,211 kilometres of municipal drains cannot be expected to run an advanced maintenance loop.
This is, after all, the same institution whose workers must lift heavy concrete slabs by hand simply because nobody engineered a way to clean the drains once they sealed them shut. Green infrastructure introduced into this institutional vacuum will choke within a few seasons.
Ultimately, we must overhaul our public infrastructure priorities. Success should no longer be measured by budgets disbursed or “percentage complete,” but on flood-hours avoided and homes kept dry.
True urban resilience depends less on the height of our concrete embankments and more on how intelligently we make room for water.
We have the engineering talent and the painful, firsthand experience required to fix this. The missing ingredient is the courage to stop treating our natural water bodies as prime real estate and start treating our drainage networks as an indispensable economic lifeline.
Dr Sabbir Ahmad is a tech executive with global experience in digital connectivity, sustainable infrastructure and energy, now shaping Bangladesh's semiconductor landscape as the CEO of Silicon Array Ltd. Email: sabbir@ieee.org .

item.title: The ever-rising migration fences. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Last week, at least 72 people died while attempting to reach the Spanish exclave of Ceuta from Morocco. Around 60,000 people made it into Ceuta, many of them by sea, others by climbing over border fences. Within just a few days, however, most of them had already returned to Morocco.
Both Morocco and Ceuta are located in Africa. But politically, Ceuta, like Melilla, belongs to Spain and therefore to the European Union. Europe’s response to the unprecedented influx into the exclave has been almost unanimous.
What happened has been described as a “threat to Europe’s security.” Some have even called it an “attack” or an “invasion.” Europe’s external borders, we are told, must be better protected.
Twenty-two of the European Union’s 27 member states have now signed an open letter initiated by Italy’s far-right government under Giorgia Meloni, criticizing Spain’s migration policy and calling for stricter security measures at Europe’s borders.
Italy has further suspended its Schengen agreement with Spain. That this is little more than political posturing is evident from the fact that Ceuta is not part of the Schengen Area in the first place.
While Europe appears quick to agree on yet more repression, the 72 lives irreversibly lost have become an afterthought.
Most of those who died had most of their lives still ahead of them and hoped for a better future. Instead, they found death on what they believed was the path toward that future.
As right-leaning governments across Europe compete with one another in increasingly alarmist security rhetoric, the fundamental question is largely ignored: Why does a young person take such enormous risks in order to reach Europe?
People flee war, violence, persecution, poverty, and the hopelessness that arises when there is little prospect of a safe and dignified life.
Border fences cannot deter those who see no viable future where they are, but merely make their journeys more dangerous and more deadly.
One can debate at length the respective roles played by colonialism and other historical injustices on the one hand, and current political failures on the other, in creating global inequality.
But this does not change the fact that a young person in Morocco, facing high youth unemployment and low wages, has every reason to perceive their situation as profoundly unjust when compared with life in much of Europe.
This inequality is not an abstract concept. In a world where everyone is connected to everyone else, and our planet, in many ways, has become a global village, it is experienced directly. People see how others live on their phone screens every day.
19-year-old Nok in Thailand can watch in real time as Moritz, her age and from Munich, spontaneously buys a flight ticket to Bangkok and spends six months travelling through Southeast Asia to “find himself.”
A comparable journey to Europe is out of reach for Nok, given her limited financial means and the enormous difficulty of obtaining a Schengen visa, and it will remain an impossibility in the foreseeable future.
“Come through legal channels,” Europe tells migrants. Kwame in Ghana wants nothing more than to do exactly that. He successfully applies for a Master’s program in Germany, spends months of his time and a considerable amount of money on language tests, certifications, translations, and other documents he needs for his visa application, and saves the required funds for his living expenses in Germany.
Yet when he requests an appointment at the German Embassy in Accra, he learns that the waiting time is six to 12 months. He will miss the start of his program. Whether his admission will still be valid the following year remains uncertain.
Amina is eight years old and lives in Sudan. For months, there has been little to no schooling in her region. The healthcare system has largely collapsed. While her parents struggle every day to find enough food and clean water, many children in Europe take education, healthcare, and security for granted.
José is 24 years old and works 12 hours a day in a textile factory in Honduras for a wage that barely allows him to survive. The clothes he sews are later sold in Europe, often for more money than he earns in an entire week.
Nok, Kwame, Amina, and José had no control over where they were born. Neither did Moritz. Yet the consequences of this accident of birth could hardly be more different.
It may be easier to demand higher fences, but as long as such extreme inequalities in security, prosperity, and future opportunities exist between different regions of the world, people will continue trying to overcome those fences.
The challenges of migration cannot be solved by sealing oneself off. They require an honest debate about how the global order can be made fairer.
This is not simply a matter of extending humanitarian compassion as a voluntary gesture; it is a question of how much inequality can be morally justified when it is based largely on the accident of where someone happens to be born.
If Europe wants to prevent images like those from Ceuta in the future, it must address the root causes of migration more decisively -- among other things through fairer trade relations, greater commitment to development cooperation, and the expansion of legal migration pathways.
Paradoxically, the opposite trend can often be observed today. Many European countries, for example, have significantly reduced their development aid budgets in recent years -- a sign of the growing influence of populism, which prioritizes short-term political gains over long-term solutions.
Ultimately, such policies harm not only people in countries of origin, but Europe itself as well.
Rainer Ebert holds a PhD in Philosophy from Rice University in Texas and is a Research Fellow at the University of South Africa. He can be reached at rainerebert.com .

item.title: Rod Liddle played the politics of hatred - we should be honest about his legacy. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Rod Liddle played the politics of hatred - we should be honest about his legacy

Submitted by Peter Oborne on Wed, 08/05/2026 - 11:05
Tributes praised a 'great journalist', but very few touched on the fact that he was also a racist, a bigot and an Islamophobe
'Truth-teller for our times', or racist and bigot? Newspaper columnist Rod Liddle (Photo/X)
Off

This year, few public figures have enjoyed as resounding a send-off as the newspaper columnist Rod Liddle.

Mr Liddle, who died this week, is being hailed as a truth-teller for our times whose trenchant columns "upset all the right people".  

There’s no denying that Liddle was a sometimes dazzling writer who grabbed the reader’s attention and never let it go. 

Many tributes have emphasised this heaven-sent quality, and many have added that a kindly soul lurked behind the intimidating public personality.

But very few tributes even touched on the fact that Liddle was also a racist, a bigot and an Islamophobe. This open and undisguised bigotry was a core part of his public identity, his personality and his legacy.

"I have spent the morning trying to draw a cartoon of a black person without it being racist," Liddle opened one column for the Spectator. He went on: "It’s bloody difficult. Especially the lips."

In another Spectator article he falsely claimed that the "overwhelming majority" of violent crime in London was carried out by young African-Caribbean men.

Genocide denial

On Tuesday, this kind of writing was hailed as brilliant right across the British media and political establishment

Fraser Nelson, who as editor of the Spectator published hundreds of Liddle’s articles, said that "his jokes were built on judgment, rigour, compassion". 

But is this true?

Pride with a dash of prejudice: How the Spectator embraced the narrative of anti-Muslim bigotry
Read More »

Take, for example, Liddle’s public defence of Myanmar’s massacre of Rohingya Muslims. On the pages of the Sun in September, 2017, he asked:"Are you sure we’re being told the full story about those Muslim Rohingya refugees who are flooding into Bangladesh from Burma? "All we get is a BBC correspondent crying in front of the refugee camps every night.

"It’s probably true that the Burmese government has been a bit, um, heavy-handed. But shouldn’t we be told a little more about the causes of the problem?"

Myanmar, bear in mind, is now charged with genocide.

It is well-documented that Burmese militias, backed by the army, had gone through Myanmar’s Rakhine province on a systematic campaign of slaughter, rape and destruction. 

In the immediate aftermath of the events that Liddle dismisses so lightly, I travelled to neighbouring Bangladesh to get the stories of survivors.

One witness told me that the first action of soldiers upon arriving at his Rohingya village was to separate the local people into three groups. 

Men, young women (including girls as young as five), old women or those one eyewitness described to me as "those who are not so beautiful." 

The soldiers opened fire. "All the young men were shot at once. It took less than ten minutes," the eyewitness told me. The soldiers then walked over to the pile of dead bodies. Anyone who showed signs of life was hacked to death with a machete. The soldiers then opened fire on the older women.

Finally the younger women were then taken to the forest and gang-raped, before being burnt alive. This process was described by Liddle - long after all this was well-documented - as "a bit, um, heavy-handed".

The slaughter of the Rohingya was one of the most heinous crimes of the 21st century. Liddle used it to fill a jokey column in the Sun. 

This wasn’t a joke. It was genocide denial. 

Normalising hate

Liddle mocked, ridiculed and sneered at pretty well every minority group, but he reserved a special contempt for Muslims. 

"A quick update on what the Muslim savages are up to," began one of Liddle’s "hilarious" articles. 

Did Rod Liddle use his remarkable talents to leave the world a better and kinder place? I am not certain he did

As election fever grew in the autumn of 2019 Liddle confided to Spectator readers that, "My own choice of election date would be a day when universities are closed and Muslims are forbidden to do anything on pain of hell, or something." He explained: "That would deliver at least 40 seats to the Tories, I reckon."

Many of the tributes paid yesterday to Liddle emphasised his courage in mocking the establishment.

I’m not sure that’s right. In one Spectator article, he recalled how on a country walk he spotted a sign urging walkers to respect the Countryside Code.

The notice was illustrated by a picture of a woman wearing a burka. Liddle told his readers that the burka was "a coded message saying, essentially, this: 'You think this is your country, you sap? It is not. It is not even your country up here among the beech hangers and the silver birch and the purple ragwort and the fluttering brimstones. Even up here, it is not yours. Not any more. Get used to this new reality, quickly.'"

We shouldn’t deceive ourselves that this racist rant was a joke.

Liddle was playing the politics of hatred, using  "humour" to tell Spectator readers that women in burkas are invaders who don’t belong in our country.

Elsewhere, Liddle dismissed the London borough of Tower Hamlets, home to a substantial Bangladeshi Muslim community, as a "fly-blown satrapy" and "suburb of Sylhet".

How UK news and politics are in the grip of an ‘Islamist’ conspiracy theory
Read More »

No wonder Rupert Lowe, leader of the racist Restore party, which calls for the mass deportation of immigrants, yesterday hailed Liddle as a "towering intellect and a friend".

"Islamophobia?" Liddle once rhetorically asked. "Count me in."

More recently one of Liddle’s articles carried the sub-headline "There’s not enough Islamophobia in the Conservative Party." After an outcry the Spectator changed the headline.

One only has to imagine the career-ending consequences for Liddle had he asserted that “there’s not enough antisemitism in the Labour Party.”

Spectator editor Michael Gove responded to the news of Liddle’s death as follows:"Rod Liddle was a journalist of genius. In the tradition of Swift, Cobbett and Orwell, he was a satirist who found society’s most sensitive spots and made merciless fun of our follies."

Gove is wrong. Jonathan Swift, William Cobbett and George Orwell, to adapt a longstanding reporters’ phrase, understood that their task was to "comfort the afflicted and afflict the comfortable".

Liddle targeted the weak and vulnerable, focusing especially on immigrants. His defenders argue that he was standing up for former working-class voters who have been forgotten and ignored by our main political parties.

It is true that they were forgotten for many years, and that Liddle gave them some kind of voice. 

Legacy of racism

The criticism of Liddle concerns the way he set about it. 

He targeted the immigrants themselves rather than focusing on the deep inequalities and injustices in British society that have left traditional working-class communities without hope and a decent future.

In this context, it is telling that his work invariably appeared in the oligarch media, whether the Murdoch press or the Spectator.

On Tuesday, the Times, which is owned by Murdoch, gave two full pages of praise for Rod Liddle. None of them dealt seriously with his racism, Islamophobia and the lazy, bigoted ignorance that caused him to deny the Myanmar genocide. 

The gush from mainstream journalists and politicians like Nick Robinson, Jeremy Vine, Andrew Neil, Fraser Nelson, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, Reform leader Nigel Farage, Iain Dale, Robert Jenrick and many others makes me wonder whether something has changed fundamentally - and for the worse - about British society.

Samir Shah praised Liddle as a "warm-hearted and generous fellow", with no mention of his trademark bigotry and racism. This was a serious error of judgment from the chairman of the BBC. 

Nearly 30 years have passed since the British politician Enoch Powell died. The obituaries rightly paid tribute to his formidable intellect, his exemplary war record, his political courage and much more besides.

Mainstream writers, politicians or broadcasters have either ignored Liddle’s racism and bigotry or dismissed it as a side issue, or even as a 'joke'

But they also examined at length the repugnant racist views which caused Edward Heath to sack him from the Tory shadow cabinet.

Yet, mainstream writers, politicians or broadcasters have either ignored Liddle’s racism and bigotry or dismissed it as a side issue, or even as a "joke". 

Years ago in the Spectator magazine, I was a colleague of Rod Liddle. Sometimes he would turn out for my cricket team. He was amusing company and I think everybody liked him.

He was clever and sharp and less disorganised and shambolic than he pretended. He was a performer and he made us all laugh. And it’s true he could write hypnotically well. 

But is that enough to make a great journalist, as so many have labelled him?

Rod undeniably had significant and unusual gifts. With such gifts comes responsibility and I wonder whether he used them well.

Did Rod Liddle use his remarkable talents to leave the world a better and kinder place? I am not certain he did.

item.title: The unfinished revolution. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Two years after the July 2024 r evolution, Bangladesh continues to honour the courage and sacrifice of those who lost their lives and the thousands more who were injured during one of the most consequential popular movements in the nation’s history.
The commemorations have rightly celebrated the resilience of ordinary citizens who stood up against what they believed to be injustice.
Yet amid the speeches, memorials, and public reflections, one important aspect of the movement deserves greater attention.
The July Revolution is now widely remembered as a struggle for d emocracy. It undoubtedly became one. But that is not how it began.
Its immediate trigger was the controversy surrounding the q uota s ystem in public-sector recruitment.
Beneath that issue, however, lay a much deeper national anxiety -- an anxiety about fairness itself.
For many young Bangladeshis, the protests reflected a growing belief that opportunities in public life were increasingly shaped by political affiliation, patronage, influence, and personal connections rather than by competence, integrity, and hard work.
The q uota issue was therefore not the destination; it was the point of departure.
What emerged during those extraordinary weeks in 2024 was something much larger: A demand that Bangladesh become a society where merit matters.
At its heart, the movement posed a simple but profound question: S hould a citizen’s future depend primarily on talent and effort, or on political loyalty and privileged access?
That question remains just as relevant in 2026 as it was in July 2024.
Political transitions often create the illusion that changing governments automatically changes governance. History suggests otherwise.
Governments may change overnight; institutions seldom do.
Elections determine who occupies public office, but institutions determine how power is exercised long after election campaigns have ended.
The enduring significance of the July movement therefore lies not only in the political changes it produced but in the institutional questions it raised.
Will Bangladesh build a r epublic where public institutions command confidence because they are fair, impartial, and professionally managed?
Or will successive governments continue to inherit -- and perhaps reshape -- the same structures of patronage that have weakened public trust for decades?
This is the u nfinished r evolution.
Democracy n eeds m eritocracy
A democratic society derives its legitimacy from more than free elections. Citizens judge the quality of their democracy through everyday encounters with public institutions.
When institutions are trusted, democracy acquires depth and resilience.
When they are not, elections risk becoming little more than contests over who controls the machinery of the state.
This is why meritocracy should never be viewed as a narrow administrative concept. It is, in fact, one of democracy’s essential foundations.
Meritocracy does not imply that societies should ignore questions of equity or historical disadvantage. Every nation must balance inclusion with excellence.
Public policy should ensure that disadvantaged communities have genuine opportunities to compete.
But equality of opportunity is fundamentally different from permanent systems that undermine public confidence in fairness.
Citizens must believe that the rules apply equally to everyone.
Without that confidence, institutions gradually lose legitimacy, regardless of which political party happens to govern.
Institutions m atter m ore t han i ndividuals
The history of successful nations demonstrates a remarkably consistent lesson. Prosperity depends less upon natural resources than upon institutional quality.
Countries blessed with abundant resources have frequently remained poor because their institutions were weak.
Others, possessing few natural advantages, have achieved extraordinary success by building competent, professional, and politically neutral public institutions.
Singapore offers perhaps the most striking modern example. When it became independent in 1965, it lacked significant natural resources and faced profound economic uncertainty.
Its transformation into one of the world’s most effective states was driven not only by visionary leadership but by a civil service that emphasi z ed competitive recruitment, professional excellence, integrity and accountability.
South Korea’s remarkable post-war development tells a similar story. Long-term industrial planning, investment in education and technological innovation were made possible because capable public institutions could formulate policy and implement it consistently across changing political circumstances.
Even Britain’s 19th administrative reforms continue to offer useful lessons.
The British Empire was sustained by many factors, some admirable and others deeply objectionable. Colonialism itself cannot and should not be romantici z ed. Yet one institutional legacy deserves careful examination.
The British Civil Service -- and particularly the Indian Civil Service -- developed a reputation for rigorous recruitment, administrative continuity, meticulous record-keeping, and political neutrality.
British statesmen famously described it as the “steel frame” of administration because governments changed while the machinery of governance continued to function.
Independent nations across the Commonwealth rightly rejected imperial rule while retaining many of those administrative principles.
The lesson remains relevant today.
Efficient government depends upon transparent recruitment. Professional administration depends upon political neutrality. Institutional credibility depends upon integrity.
These are not colonial values or Western values. They are universal principles of good governance.
Bangladesh’s own Constitution envisages a r epublic governed through accountable public institutions operating under the rule of law.
Meritocracy is therefore not an imported ideal. It is a constitutional necessity.
Mohiuddin Zaman is a retired Canadian banking executive of Bangladeshi origin. He has lived overseas for 40 years but always remained deeply connected to Bangladesh.

item.title: Two years later. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Two years after the events of August 5 and the July Revolution of 2024, our nation stands at a moment that demands both honest reflection and determination moving forward.
What we collectively experienced will unquestionably remain one of the most monumental days in our nation’s history as we saw the fall of Sheikh Hasina’s government after over a decade and a half.
To say it was an unprecedented event would be minimizing its impact, one that began as student-led demonstrations over unfair job quota systems but eventually escalated into a nationwide uprising against a regime that the people of this country no longer had the patience and tolerance for. A regime that became synonymous not just with deep public frustration with governance, inequality, and institutional fragility, but also with mistreatment of the very people it swore to serve.
However, two years removed, Bangladesh is a new country, and intends to be a better nation. However, we continue to face some of the same issues that have plagued us throughout our history, and indeed continue to hold us back from taking that next step in our evolution.
The general election of February 2026, which brought the BNP to power, marked yet another significant political shift after Dr Yunus’s interim government looked to steady the nation post August 2024. The election, widely seen as arguably the interim government’s most significant achievement, also reflected a public desire for change, stability, and competent administration.
However, political transition alone cannot resolve the entrenched problems that fuelled the unrest of 2024. Citizens expect delivery, not rhetoric and reform, not excuses.
The BNP government led by Tarique Rahman inherits a nation that is impatient for results and, as our very recent history has shown, is unwilling to tolerate the complacency that has long plagued our public life. As such, all those within the government must shy away from complacency, and instead work to serve the best interests of the general public.
At present, our challenges in gas and energy, healthcare, and education are among the more salient and immediate concerns that the government must prioritize. While the ongoing measles outbreak is a crisis that should never have happened, and the interim government must rightly be criticized for its failure, we must continue to do all we can to stop this senseless loss of life.
The gas and energy crisis is another test of the state’s capacity to deliver, and is an indictment of our failure to diversify our energy mix while also relying too heavily on imported power. Our energy system has long needed structural reform: Diversified sources, transparent procurement, better planning, and accelerated investment in renewables. Without a stable energy foundation, any thoughts of economic recovery will remain elusive, and public frustration will deepen.
Education and unemployment too continue to cast long shadows over our future. The July Revolution was driven in part by young people demanding dignity and opportunity. Two years later, those demands remain unmet, with little to no signs of potential improvement. Bangladesh must overhaul its education system and invest in job creation, skills training, and innovation if it hopes to harness the potential of its youth while also honouring the sacrifices made during the July Revolution.
Two years on, despite the changes, we continue navigating the consequences of a political rupture that revealed deep public dissatisfaction. The February 2026 election offered a democratic reset, but the work of rebuilding trust and delivering results is far from complete.
Two years later, the lesson remains clear. We must honour those who gave their lives in the hope of a new and better Bangladesh. For that, if we are to truly build that version of Bangladesh, we must unlearn many of the ways this nation has functioned since its inception.

item.title: A July-to-July reflection: Reimagining education after crisis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is 36th July again.
In July 2024 , Bangladesh witnessed a student led protest turning into an uprising. Our regular class-goers called for a change, not in class schedules or in the university’s setting but in a system that had been denying fairness in the name of social equity. A long-practiced system of doing unjust to our students in the name of quota system. The protest started peacefully but the then gov ernmen t didn’t let it be peaceful for a long time. They attacked the protesters, shut down the campuses, made the students arrested and injured to stop the protest.
After two months of struggle, thousands of people’s death s and resignation of the prime minister , finally the students ’ protest saw some light. It came to an end after the fall of the political gov ernmen t. But political change did not immediately translate into educational recovery.
Going back to the classes was not easy this time. After experiencing trauma, disillusionment and a rupture in their formal education , students were hesitant to start all anew. Specially for those who led the protest from the forefront or the people who lost family, friends and relatives. Students from universities were the main stakeholders of that protest.
After the uprising when the educational institutions decided to start the operations, the experiences were particularly different for students in public universities and private universities. While many public universities remained closed for weeks due to administrative restructuring and vice-chancellor appointments, private universities resumed classes within days. These
students found themselves navigating an impossible transition from streets filled with protests to classrooms filled with deadlines or the voids of the beloved classmates. They were expected to move from resistance to routine without being given the space to process what they had lived through.
Yet this difficult moment also revealed something important. A few private universities recognized that education after a crisis could not simply be about covering missed syllabi. They adjusted academic calendars, redesigned classroom activities, created spaces for dialogue, offered psychological support, and acknowledged that learning cannot happen when students are emotionally disconnected from themselves and their communities. These responses, though limited, pointed toward a different understanding of education, that values care alongside curriculum.
Some private universities made flexible deadlines, reduced academic pressure and offered counseling services while others made the journey smoother by intriguing trauma-informed pedagogy and crisis-responsive academic policies. The question, then, was not how quickly universities can return to normal. The question was whether "normal" was ever enough.
As parts of the healing process few academic programs used projects, unconventional academic duties and planned creative engagement of the students. When the universities started their operations, students were no longer confined to passive roles again. They were actively engaged in discussions and produced multimedia projects such as documentaries, podcasts, and digital exhibitions that captured personal and community narratives, preserved memories, and cultivated empathy. These creative efforts taught more than technical skills.
They instilled a deep understanding of how to handle sensitive issues with care and how to communicate with purpose in an era overwhelmed by misinformation. Few of the universities adapted the curriculums expanded rapidly to include civic education, digital literacy, and trauma-informed practices, bridging the gap between academic content and lived experiences.
Classroom walls became porous, allowing the realities outside to shape the learning inside, with student voices and local stories taking center stage. This shift from rote learning to responsive, student-centered education was supported and appreciated by both university authorities’ grassroots efforts and students, signaling a move toward a more compassionate and socially aware model of teaching. Education became a powerful tool not only for academic development but also for community rebuilding, emotional resilience, and civic engagement.
The July movement initially challenged political institutions, but it also challenged educational institutions. It reminded us that universities are not merely degree-producing spaces. They are communities where students develop civic responsibility, critical thinking, and collective identity. When those communities experience crisis, recovery must involve more than reopening gates and resuming examinations.
As we mark two years since those unforgettable days, perhaps the greatest lesson is this: E ducation must become more resilient, more humane, and more responsive. Universities need crisis-informed pedagogy, accessible mental health support, flexible academic policies, and classrooms where reflection is considered as important as instruction. Learning after conflict requires healing before performance.
July 2024 changed the political history of Bangladesh. Whether it also changes the future of higher education depends on what universities choose to learn from it. Years later, July is not simply a reminder of what students have achieved. It is also a reminder of what education still needs to become.
Tanjila Habib is a lecturer at the School of General Education in BRAC University. She can be reached at tanjila.habib@bracu.ac.bd
